title: Periodic table structure and blocks; Metallic bonding and comparing structures; Ionic bonding and lattices
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Edexcel A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: BD06#t4 term and clue written for the game; BD06#t3 term and clue written for the game; PT01#t1 term and clue written for the game; PT01#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: BD01#N.3a, BD06#N.3a, PT01#N.6, BD01#N.6, BD06#N.11, PT01#N.12a, BD01#N.12a, BD06#N.13, BD01#N.14a, BD06#N.15, BD01#N.15.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Ductile
items.clue: Able to be drawn into wires, because layers of ions slide.

items.label: Malleable
items.clue: Able to be hammered into shape, because layers of ions slide.

items.label: Period
items.clue: A row of the table; its number gives the outer occupied shell.

items.label: Valence electrons
items.clue: The outer-shell particles of an atom: seven for bromine, 4s² 4p⁵.

questions.stem: An atom of element X has the electron configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴. Which ion does X form in its ionic compounds?

options.text: X²⁺
X⁶⁺
X²⁻
X⁶⁻

questions.explanation: Six outer electrons (3s² 3p⁴). X gains two to reach 3s² 3p⁶: 16 protons, 18 electrons, charge 2−. X is sulfur: S²⁻.

questions.stem: Aluminium is rolled into kitchen foil less than 0.02 mm thick without cracking. Which statement explains this property of aluminium?

options.text: Its layers of cations slide, staying attracted to the delocalised electrons around them.
Its metallic bonds are weak, so the rollers can easily push its atoms apart.
Its bonds between neighbouring atoms bend like hinges instead of breaking.
Its individual atoms are soft, so each one is flattened as it passes between the rollers.

questions.explanation: Metallic bonding is non-directional, so the delocalised electrons keep attracting the cations after the layers have slid. The metal changes shape without cracking.

questions.stem: Germanium is in period 4, group 14. Which is the full electron configuration of a germanium atom?

options.text: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 4p²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d² 4s²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁴

questions.explanation: Period 4, p-block: fill up to 4p. Group 14 gives 14 − 10 = 4 valence electrons, 4s² 4p². With the 3d¹⁰, the total is 32 electrons.

options.text: NH₄SO₄ for ammonium sulfate
NaCO₃ for sodium carbonate
Ca(OH)₂ for calcium hydroxide
AlNO₃ for aluminium nitrate

questions.explanation: One Ca²⁺ (2+) is balanced by two OH⁻ (2 × 1−). The bracket keeps each hydroxide ion whole.

questions.stem: Four solids, P, Q, R and S, are tested. - P: melts at 801 °C; conducts when molten but not as a solid; dissolves in water. - Q: melts at 1085 °C; conducts as a solid and when molten; insoluble in water. - R: melts at 114 °C; does not conduct as a solid or when molten; insoluble in water. - S: melts at 1710 °C; does not conduct as a solid or when molten; insoluble in water. Which pairing of substance and structure is correct?

options.text: P is metallic, because it conducts when molten.
Q is ionic, because it conducts when molten.
R is molecular, because it melts low and never conducts.
S is ionic, because its melting point is very high.

questions.stem: Beryllium, 1s² 2s², and helium, 1s², both have two electrons in their outer s sub-shell. Why is beryllium placed in group 2, but helium in group 18?

options.text: Beryllium is a solid and helium is a gas, and group 18 holds the gaseous elements.
Beryllium has four electrons and helium two, and the group number counts the total.
Beryllium's 2s² electrons are in a higher shell, so they are inner electrons, not valence electrons.
Beryllium's outer shell, n = 2, is far from full, while helium's n = 1 shell is full with just two.

questions.stem: Sodium chloride has a very low volatility: it does not evaporate at room temperature and melts only at 801 °C. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Every ion is strongly attracted to many ions of opposite charge.
Its particles are so heavy that they cannot move fast enough to escape.
Evaporating it would break the strong bond in every NaCl molecule.
Sodium is a metal with a high boiling point, and NaCl keeps this property.

questions.explanation: Each ion is surrounded by oppositely charged ions and attracted to all of them. Separating them means overcoming many strong attractions.

questions.stem: Silicon melts at 1414 °C. Phosphorus (white, P₄) melts at 44 °C. Which statement explains the difference?

options.text: Phosphorus has weaker metallic bonding, because its atoms are larger than silicon atoms.
Silicon is giant covalent, so covalent bonds break; phosphorus is P₄ molecules held by weak London forces.
Melting phosphorus breaks its P–P covalent bonds, which are much weaker than Si–Si bonds.
Silicon atoms have more electrons than P₄ molecules, so London forces between them are stronger.

questions.explanation: Melting silicon breaks strong Si–Si covalent bonds throughout the lattice. Melting P₄ overcomes only weak forces between molecules; the P–P bonds stay intact.

questions.stem: Ionic radii (pm): Na⁺ 102, K⁺ 138, F⁻ 133, Cl⁻ 181. Which shows the strength of the ionic bonding in NaF, NaCl and KCl in decreasing order?

options.text: KCl > NaCl > NaF
NaF > NaCl > KCl
NaF > KCl > NaCl
NaF = NaCl = KCl

questions.explanation: All are 1+ and 1−, so radii decide. Radius sums: NaF 235, NaCl 283, KCl 319 pm. Closer centres, stronger attraction.

questions.stem: Each liquid is tested with two electrodes and a bulb. Which liquid will not conduct electricity?

options.text: Molten sodium chloride at 850 °C
Liquid mercury at 20 °C
Liquid titanium(IV) chloride, TiCl₄, at 20 °C
Molten aluminium at 700 °C

questions.explanation: TiCl₄ (boils at 136 °C) is made of small covalent molecules. With no ions and no delocalised electrons, nothing carries charge, even though titanium is a metal.

questions.stem: In a kettle's heating element, the hot metal wire is packed in powdered magnesium oxide, MgO, inside a metal tube. MgO is ionic, yet it is used here as an electrical insulator. Why doesn't it conduct?

options.text: MgO contains no ions until it is dissolved or melted.
Its ions are held in fixed positions, and MgO stays solid at the element's temperature.
Its electrons are all shared in covalent bonds, so none are free to move.
Its ions are too highly charged to move, even when MgO is molten.

questions.explanation: Charge flows only if charged particles can move. In the solid the ions are locked in the lattice and there are no free electrons. Strong 2+/2− attractions keep MgO solid to about 2850 °C.
